markdown.headingText: Are home buyers inattentive towards energy efficiency?
markdown.markdown:
::::::::: hero ::: hero-eyebrow Master's Thesis · Applied Economics and Data Science ::: ::: hero-subtitle An econometric analysis based on a new data set created with NLP and OCR techniques. ::: :::::: hero-meta ::: hero-meta-item **Author** Valdimar Einarsson ::: ::: hero-meta-item **Data span** 2010 – 2023 ::: ::: hero-meta-item **Final sample** 728,794 observations ::: :::::: ::::::::: ## Overview {.unnumbered} ::: paratext On this site, I present my empirical project, conducted as part of my Master's thesis in Applied Economics and Data Science. In this project, I attempt to determine whether homebuyers in Denmark value energy efficiency and specific energy-related features in properties. In particular, I explore whether homebuyers are willing to pay a premium for energy-efficient properties or, conversely, accept a discount for properties that are less energy-efficient. To quantify energy efficiency, both the energy label or EPC label (i.e. the label stated in the Energy Performance Certificate of each property) and estimated energy consumption in kWh were utilised. Furthermore, the impact of different energy heat sources and three energy systems — specifically, properties with heat pumps, solar panels, and solar heating — on property prices was examined. ::: ## Research context {.unnumbered} ::: paratext In recent decades, addressing climate change has become increasingly urgent. Among the high-emission sectors, the **building industry** is estimated to be responsible for roughly **40% of global CO₂ emissions**, of which about 70% is generated by building operations and 30% by construction activities. In the European Union, the building sector accounted for approximately **35% of energy-related emissions** in 2021. In 2002, the EU introduced the **Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD)** to promote energy efficiency, introducing **Energy Performance Certificates (EPC)** to close the information gap between property owners and prospective buyers and to correct behavioural failures such as decision-making heuristics and biases. A **2010 recast** required Member States to display the energy performance indicator — the A to G label — in any commercial real-estate advertisement. Between 2005 and 2021, total CO₂ emissions from the EU building sector dropped by **31%**. Denmark has had mandatory energy certification since **1997**, making it one of the first EU countries to implement an EPC scheme. Yet no measurable impact on the Danish real-estate market was observed until **2011**, one year after the EPBD recast. Existing Danish evidence remains limited, with the most recent research dating to **2016**, and few studies use the additional information available in the EPC reports — such as renovation recommendations, renovation cost, investment cost, and the potential energy label a property could achieve. ::: ## Contributions {.unnumbered} ::::::::: grid :::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-4} ::: feature-card ### Coverage The first paper to account for **all residential property types** in Denmark. To the best of our knowledge, all studies that investigate the Danish housing market have focused only on detached houses. ::: :::: :::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-4} ::: feature-card ### Renovation potential Beyond the energy label and energy consumption, the analysis incorporates **additional information from the EPC reports** related to renovation potentials towards energy efficiency. If consumers pay attention to the EPC reports and are willing to pay a premium for energy-efficient properties — hence a discount for non-efficient ones — that premium or discount may vary with the renovation potential a property can achieve. ::: :::: :::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-4} ::: feature-card ### Policy effect The analysis measures the effect of **tighter policy implementation** on the Danish housing market. Danish authorities implemented tighter building regulations on **1 January 2018**, setting minimum energy performance requirements for all new buildings and minimum energy-efficiency requirements for renovations of existing buildings. ::: :::: ::::::::: ## Project at a glance {.unnumbered} ::::::::::::::: stat-grid ::::: stat-card ::: stat-number 2,295,344 ::: ::: stat-label Property transactions and characteristics scraped ::: ::::: ::::: stat-card ::: stat-number 776,108 ::: ::: stat-label EPC PDF documents processed ::: ::::: ::::: stat-card ::: stat-number 728,794 ::: ::: stat-label Final observations after merging and cleaning ::: ::::: ::::: stat-card ::: stat-number 2010 – 2023 ::: ::: stat-label Sample period ::: ::::: ::::::::::::::: ## Thesis roadmap {.unnumbered} :::::::: roadmap ::: roadmap-item **Chapter 2 — EPBD and the Danish EPC scheme** Introduces the implementation of the Energy Performance Certificates in Denmark and the structure of the reports. ::: ::: roadmap-item **Chapter 3 — Literature review** Reviews the literature related to this paper. ::: ::: roadmap-item **Chapter 4 — Data** Gives a detailed description of the data and how it was obtained. ::: ::: roadmap-item **Chapter 5 — Empirical strategy** Outlines the theory of the hedonic model and the empirical strategy utilised in this paper. ::: ::: roadmap-item **Chapter 6 — Results** Presents the results. ::: :::::::: ## Programming languages used and their functions ```{=html}
Python R
- Data cleaning and pre-processing - Data visualization
- Web scraping - Regression modelling
- PDF parsing (The EPC reports)
- Text classification models (NLP)
- Optical character recognition (OCR)
- Geographical data extraction
``` ## Tooling and data by function ```{=html}

Source code is available on [GitHub](https://github.com/valdikaldi/Empirical_Project-are_home_buyers_inattentive_towards_energy_efficiency). :::
